items.readable_text:
Content:
Let [MATH: T_P] and [MATH: T_Q] be the truth sets of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),] respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

Content:
The implication of the predicates [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] is a new predicate that we denote as follows:
[MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \Rightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)]

Content:
This implication is false whenever [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is true and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is false for a specific set of respective variable assignments [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.]

Content:
Now, recall the following logical equivalence:

Content:
[MATH: P\Rightarrow Q \equiv \lnot P \lor Q]

Content:
Therefore, the truth set of [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] is given by

Content:
[MATH: T_{P⇒Q}|= T_{¬P∨Q}; = T_{¬P}∪T_{Q}; = T^(―)_{P}∪T_{Q}.]

Content:
For example, suppose we have the following universal set:

Content:
[MATH: U = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 \big\}]

Content:
Let's define the following predicates over [MATH: U{:}]

Content:
- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is prime
- [MATH: Q(x):] [MATH: 9] is divisible by [MATH: x]

Content:
To find the truth set of [MATH: P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x),] we note the following:

Content:
- The truth set of [MATH: P(x)] is [MATH: T_P = \left\{ 2,3,5,7 \right\}.] As a result, the complement is
[MATH: T^(―)_{P} = {2, 3, 5, 7}^(―) = {1, 4, 6, 8, 9}.]
- The truth set of [MATH: Q(x)] is
[MATH: T_Q = \big\{ 1,3,9 \big\}.]

Content:
Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: T_{P⇒Q}|= T^(―)_{P}∪T_{Q}; = {1, 4, 6, 8, 9}∪{1, 3, 9}; = {1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9}.]

sections.normalized_html:
• The following statement is an equivalence (i.e., it is true). [MATH: x + 2 = 5 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=3] This statement is true because [MATH: \left(x+2=5\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=3\right)\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \left(x=3\quad\Rightarrow\quad x+2 = 5\right).]

  • The following statement is not an equivalence (i.e., it is false). [MATH: x^2 = 4 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=2] This statement is false because [MATH: \left(x=2 \quad \Rightarrow\quad x^2 = 4\right) \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \left(x^2=4\quad \not\Rightarrow\quad x=2\right).] However, the following statement is true: [MATH: x^2 = 4 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=\pm 2]

Let [MATH: T_P] and [MATH: T_Q] be the truth sets of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),] respectively. Again, we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

Content:
The equivalence of the predicates [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] is a new predicate that we denote as follows:
[MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \Leftrightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)]

Content:
This predicate is true when [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] have the same truth values for a specific set of variable assignments [MATH: x_1,x_2,\ldots, x_n.]

Content:
[MATH: P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)]

Content:
Let's look at some examples. Assume [MATH: x\in\mathbb R] throughout.

Content:
- The following statement is an equivalence (i.e., it is true).
[MATH: x + 2 = 5 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=3]
This statement is true because
[MATH: \left(x+2=5\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=3\right)\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \left(x=3\quad\Rightarrow\quad x+2 = 5\right).]
- The following statement is not an equivalence (i.e., it is false).
[MATH: x^2 = 4 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=2]
This statement is false because
[MATH: \left(x=2 \quad \Rightarrow\quad x^2 = 4\right) \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \left(x^2=4\quad \not\Rightarrow\quad x=2\right).]
However, the following statement is true:
[MATH: x^2 = 4 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=\pm 2]

For predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),] the equivalence [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\Leftrightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is true when [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] have the same truth value.

Content:
[MATH: P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)]

Content:
It follows that the truth set of [MATH: P \Leftrightarrow Q] can be found using

Content:
[MATH: T_{P⇔Q} = (T_{P}∩T_{Q})∪(T^(―)_{P}∩T^(―)_{Q}).]

Content:
Let's find the truth set of [MATH: P(x) \Leftrightarrow Q(x)] given the following predicates defined over the universal set [MATH: \mathbb{R}{:}]

Content:
- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: 1-5x < 11]
- [MATH: Q(x):] [MATH: x \geq -1]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- To find the the truth set of [MATH: P(x),] we solve the corresponding inequality:
[MATH: 1 − 5x|< 11; − 5x|< 10; x|> − 2]
So, the truth set of [MATH: P(x)] is [MATH: T_P = (-2, \infty)] and its complement is [MATH: \overline{T}_P = (-\infty,-2].]
- The truth set of [MATH: Q(x)] is [MATH: T_Q = [-1, \infty)] and its complement is [MATH: \overline{T}_Q = (-\infty,-1).]

Content:
Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: T_{P}∩T_{Q}|= (− 2, ∞)∩[− 1, ∞); = [− 1, ∞); T^(―)_{P}∩T^(―)_{Q}|= (− ∞, − 2]∩(− ∞, − 1); = (− ∞, − 2]; T_{P⇔Q}|= (T_{P}∩T_{Q})∪(T^(―)_{P}∩T^(―)_{Q}); = [− 1, ∞)∪(− ∞, − 2]; = (− ∞, − 2]∪[− 1, ∞).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since we have that

[MATH: P(x) \Leftrightarrow Q(x) \equiv \big(P(x) \land Q(x)\big) \lor \big(\neg P(x) \land \neg Q(x)\big),] the corresponding truth set can be found as follows:

[MATH: T_{P⇔Q} = (T_{P}∩T_{Q})∪(T^(―)_{P}∩T^(―)_{Q})]

Notice that:

  • The truth set of [MATH: P(x)] is [MATH: T_P = \big\{ 2,4,6,8,10 \big\}] and its complement is [MATH: \overline{T}_P %= \overline{\big\{ 4,6,8,9,10 \big\}} = \big\{1,3,5,7,9 \big\}.]

  • The truth set of [MATH: Q(x)] is [MATH: T_Q = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,6 \big\}] and its complement is [MATH: \overline{T}_Q %= \overline{\big\{ \big\}} = \big\{ 5,7,8,9,10 \big\}.]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: T_{P}∩T_{Q}|= {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}∩{1, 2, 3, 4, 6}; = {2, 4, 6}; T^(―)_{P}∩T^(―)_{Q}|= {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}∩{5, 7, 8, 9, 10}; = {5, 7, 9}; T_{P⇔Q}|= (T_{P}∩T_{Q})∪(T^(―)_{P}∩T^(―)_{Q}); = {2, 4, 6}∪{5, 7, 9}; = {2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9}.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Since implication and equivalence of predicates are simply generalizations of logical operations on statements, all the properties of these operations can be translated to the corresponding operations on predicates.

Content:
In particular, for predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),] we have the following:

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q|≡¬P∨Q; P⇔Q|≡(P⇒Q)∧(Q⇒P); ≡(¬P∨Q)∧(¬Q∨P); ≡(¬P∧¬Q)∨(P∧Q)]

Content:
Finally, let's remind ourselves of the grammatical constructions for implications and biconditionals that we've encountered so far:

Content:
For conditional statements, the following are equivalent:

Content:
- [MATH: P\Rightarrow Q]
- If [MATH: P,] then [MATH: Q]
- [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q]

Content:
For biconditional statements, the following are equivalent:

Content:
- [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q]
- [MATH: P] is equivalent to [MATH: Q]
- [MATH: P] if and only if [MATH: Q]
- If [MATH: P] then [MATH: Q,] and if [MATH: Q] then [MATH: P]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let [MATH: T_P] and [MATH: T_Q] be the truth sets of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),] respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

Content:
The implication of the predicates [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] is a new predicate that we denote as follows:
[MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \Rightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)]

Content:
This implication is false whenever [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is true and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is false for a specific set of respective variable assignments [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.]

Content:
Now, recall the following logical equivalence:

Content:
[MATH: P\Rightarrow Q \equiv \lnot P \lor Q]

Content:
Therefore, the truth set of [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] is given by

Content:
[MATH: T_{P⇒Q}|= T_{¬P∨Q}; = T_{¬P}∪T_{Q}; = T^(―)_{P}∪T_{Q}.]

Content:
For example, suppose we have the following universal set:

Content:
[MATH: U = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 \big\}]

Content:
Let's define the following predicates over [MATH: U{:}]

Content:
- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is prime
- [MATH: Q(x):] [MATH: 9] is divisible by [MATH: x]

Content:
To find the truth set of [MATH: P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x),] we note the following:

Content:
- The truth set of [MATH: P(x)] is [MATH: T_P = \left\{ 2,3,5,7 \right\}.] As a result, the complement is
[MATH: T^(―)_{P} = {2, 3, 5, 7}^(―) = {1, 4, 6, 8, 9}.]
- The truth set of [MATH: Q(x)] is
[MATH: T_Q = \big\{ 1,3,9 \big\}.]

Content:
Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: T_{P⇒Q}|= T^(―)_{P}∪T_{Q}; = {1, 4, 6, 8, 9}∪{1, 3, 9}; = {1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9}.]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Equivalence of Predicates

Content:
Let [MATH: T_P] and [MATH: T_Q] be the truth sets of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),] respectively. Again, we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

Content:
The equivalence of the predicates [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] is a new predicate that we denote as follows:
[MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \Leftrightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)]

Content:
This predicate is true when [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] have the same truth values for a specific set of variable assignments [MATH: x_1,x_2,\ldots, x_n.]

Content:
[MATH: P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)]

Content:
Let's look at some examples. Assume [MATH: x\in\mathbb R] throughout.

Content:
- The following statement is an equivalence (i.e., it is true).
[MATH: x + 2 = 5 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=3]
This statement is true because
[MATH: \left(x+2=5\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=3\right)\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \left(x=3\quad\Rightarrow\quad x+2 = 5\right).]
- The following statement is not an equivalence (i.e., it is false).
[MATH: x^2 = 4 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=2]
This statement is false because
[MATH: \left(x=2 \quad \Rightarrow\quad x^2 = 4\right) \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \left(x^2=4\quad \not\Rightarrow\quad x=2\right).]
However, the following statement is true:
[MATH: x^2 = 4 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=\pm 2]

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Truth Sets of Equivalences

Content:
For predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),] the equivalence [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\Leftrightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is true when [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] have the same truth value.

Content:
[MATH: P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)]

Content:
It follows that the truth set of [MATH: P \Leftrightarrow Q] can be found using

Content:
[MATH: T_{P⇔Q} = (T_{P}∩T_{Q})∪(T^(―)_{P}∩T^(―)_{Q}).]

Content:
Let's find the truth set of [MATH: P(x) \Leftrightarrow Q(x)] given the following predicates defined over the universal set [MATH: \mathbb{R}{:}]

Content:

Item 10 — Tutorial: Logical Laws Involving Implications and Equivalences With Predicates

Content:
Since implication and equivalence of predicates are simply generalizations of logical operations on statements, all the properties of these operations can be translated to the corresponding operations on predicates.

Content:
In particular, for predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),] we have the following:

Content:
[MATH: P⇒Q|≡¬P∨Q; P⇔Q|≡(P⇒Q)∧(Q⇒P); ≡(¬P∨Q)∧(¬Q∨P); ≡(¬P∧¬Q)∨(P∧Q)]

Content:
Finally, let's remind ourselves of the grammatical constructions for implications and biconditionals that we've encountered so far:

Content:
For conditional statements, the following are equivalent:

Content:
- [MATH: P\Rightarrow Q]
- If [MATH: P,] then [MATH: Q]
- [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q]

Content:
For biconditional statements, the following are equivalent:

Content:
- [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q]
- [MATH: P] is equivalent to [MATH: Q]
- [MATH: P] if and only if [MATH: Q]
- If [MATH: P] then [MATH: Q,] and if [MATH: Q] then [MATH: P]

Item 11 — Example: Using Laws Involving Implications and Equivalences

Example Prompt:
Consider the following predicates.

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: A(x):] [MATH: x<4.] [MATH: \qquad] [MATH: B(x):] [MATH: \dfrac x2< 2.]

Which of the following is equivalent to the biconditional predicate [MATH: A(x) \Leftrightarrow B(x)?]

1. [MATH: x<4] if and only if [MATH: \dfrac x2< 2.]
2. [MATH: x<4] is equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac x2< 2.]
3. If [MATH: x<4] then [MATH: \dfrac x2< 2,] or if [MATH: \dfrac x2< 2] then [MATH: x <4.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A biconditional expression [MATH: P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv (P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P)] can be read as shown below:

- [MATH: P] if and only if [MATH: Q]
- [MATH: P] is equivalent to [MATH: Q]
- If [MATH: P] then [MATH: Q,] and if [MATH: Q] then [MATH: P]

So, [MATH: A \Leftrightarrow B] translates into the following sentences:

- [MATH: x<4] if and only if [MATH: \dfrac x2< 2.]
- [MATH: x<4] is equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac x2< 2.]
- If [MATH: x<4] then [MATH: \dfrac x2< 2,] and if [MATH: \dfrac x2< 2] then [MATH: x <4.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."
